claims.claim: Information architecture is the discipline of making information findable and understandable, covering searching, browsing, categorizing, and presenting information in websites, applications, and physical spaces.

The working definition of information architecture is the structure and labeling of information in a product: how content is organized, named, and connected; the field's foundational text is Morville and Rosenfeld's Information Architecture for the World Wide Web, and Richard Saul Wurman is credited with coining the term.

IA has four component systems: organization systems (how information is categorized and structured), labeling systems (how information and navigation options are represented), navigation systems (how users move through the structure), and search systems (how users find specific information quickly).

IA is the information backbone of a product: the underlying organization, structure, and nomenclature that define the relationships between content; it is not part of the on-screen interface but informs the UI and impacts the user experience.
IA and navigation are related but distinct: IA spans well beyond navigation, and navigation refers to the interface elements that allow users to reach specific information within the structure.

Content is more discoverable when it is not buried under multiple intervening layers; all other things being equal, deep hierarchies are more difficult to use, and a flatter hierarchy usually supports more specific labels that are easier to understand.

Organizing navigation by audience type is usually problematic: role-based IA increases cognitive effort and anxiety, and clear language with mutually exclusive categories reduces harm to the user experience.
Card sorting is a user research method that helps designers understand how users categorize and label content, so the resulting IA aligns with users' mental models.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is organizing content by audience a sound IA strategy?
positions: Audience schemes (Students / Faculty / Alumni) are one of the classic organizing schemes and let each visitor focus on content relevant to them.
Nielsen Norman Group research finds audience-based navigation is usually problematic: users often do not know which segment they belong to, and role-based IA increases cognitive effort and anxiety.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson names audience as one of the four common organizing schemes, as standard IA teaching does, but carries NN/g's caution that it is frequently the weakest choice and recommends topic- or task-based organization for most products.
